en: The *Ghaṭakarparakāvya*, accompanied by the commentary composed by the venerable Mahāmāheśvara Ācārya Śrī Abhinavaguptapāda:
"O Giver of Boons, what is this unprecedented fashioning of a crest-jewel for your head? Ah, it is understood: this bow of Smara has been scorched and placed upon your crown."
When the Goddess declared, "Upon seeing this light, the god of uneven arrows blazes forth all the more intensely," may Śambhu, his self-restraint dissolved, protect us.
This *kulaka* is spoken by a woman whose husband is away, with another woman who is also separated from her husband acting as the cause for the narration;
therein, some portions are spoken by the woman separated from her husband as portrayed by the poet, while other portions are spoken by her friend as portrayed by the poet.

We shall demonstrate its many varieties: some spoken by a messenger composed by the poet, another consisting of the speech of a counter-messenger revealed by the poet, and yet another told independently by the poet himself.
But she alone is not the one who speaks;
she whose beloved husband has gone abroad is both filled with joy and yet,
at the same time, separated from her beloved because he has departed.
Endowed with an intense intoxication born of youth and amorous passion,
her state of separation due to being in a foreign land is indicated by her being away from home;
while the orb of the sun is obscured, the manifestation of grief falls from the sky into the water.
And when the God of Love is prepared to strike at my heart, this [state] arises in one whose joy has departed due to separation from his beloved. (Ghatakarpara 1)

The sun is called *dinakara* because it makes the day; when its mass of rays is obscured or eclipsed, how can there be even mental joy or light for those women—though they are well-known as the very opposites of darkness—at the place where that sun is hidden?

Moreover, for women separated from their lovers, whose hearts are clouded by the restless longing (*raṇaraṇaka*) born of the night-time, even the day might at times become a source of kinship by bestowing the light of various diversions.
But today, by whose grace such a day arises—even that [day] has some inherent, innate nature of its own, and that too has been obscured; thus, an extreme lack of fortune is indicated.
Likewise, it falls from the sky into the water.
Of what sort is it?
It brings about sorrow (*śoka*).
For it has been heard that water indeed brings about itself through the presence of nearby terrestrial dust, uniting them as one.

But today, something unprecedented occurs: she imagines those women to be separated from their lovers through grief, and they are rendered entirely composed of sorrow. For, in the midst of the rainy season, they do not even have the slightest hope of their beloved’s return; thus, at that moment, sheer despair falls from the sky. By this, his excessive remorse is indicated, arising from the fact that this unbearable [separation] is beyond remedy.
Likewise, the God of Love is full of fury toward the striking of the heart;
whereas any external slayer might be avoided by various means, this one, however, remains stationed right within the heart and is intent upon striking from within.
The word *ca* (and) indicates simultaneity.

Just as some wicked person, finding a gap and having no one to hinder him, strikes a sorrowful person who is alone and thus vulnerable—specifically in a secluded, lightless, and gloomy day—so too, at this very time, does Madana strike such a woman of love; this is the meaning. (GhkV_1)
Having passed all this time, you clouds have arrived just when my beloved has gone;
for without me, you will surely be killed by that merciless man who dwells in a foreign land. (Ghatakarpara 2)
This is the speech of the heroine herself:
"O clouds! You who are intent on bestowing water that brings about the end of my sorrow—at that place where we were not separated from our beloveds..."

Having passed such a time, having spent it here or there, when today my beloved departed, then you arrived; thus, all this time was ordained by fate and has taken the form of death (kṛtānta). Those for whom this is so are "beyond the reach of the mind" because they cause mental distress; and they are also "clouds" (toyada)—such is the analysis of the compound.
And therefore, you shall kill me.
This is an utterance with an ironic intonation (*kākvā*):
"May I indeed become so fortunate that,
though separated from my beloved and with a heart exhausted by beholding your terrifying deeds, I may find happiness even through the abandonment of life."
Moreover, she who lives without her beloved is surely worthy of being killed;
and he who, being compassionate, dwells in a foreign land—
if he has entered the heart of his beloved— [then he too is to be pitied].
Death has already been placed in the palm of his hand;
for he is no longer capable of accomplishing any purpose during this season of the clouds. Thus, he will surely remain alone somewhere for a long time.
Therefore, let there be love toward us for now.

"If he had also shown compassion, he would certainly have come right here"—by this, it is suggested that the succession of hardships was such as to indicate the distress born from the failure of his trust. (GhkV_2)

Desiring to inform her beloved of her own condition and being unable to endure the manifestation of the terrifying clouds, the heroine—speaking with some artifice—said this with the intention: "If they should somehow depart for another land by means of these words, everything will be accomplished;
moreover, my beloved might perhaps experience my own state himself upon hearing the sound of the clouds reached in that region."
O clouds, you who swiftly traverse the path, speak to that traveler defiled by the road:
"Let your wife, who now delights in another land, be released; what more can be said? (GhK 3)
The *ghanas* are clouds;
moreover, they are exceedingly dense,
and for that very reason, they have the nature of striking.
Address that man—who is covered in dust, devoid of restraint, and merciless—amidst the travelers.
The meaning is that his very recognition is this: that he alone among the travelers is merciless.
By saying, "Since you yourselves quickly overstep the path," there is an implied encouragement [to him] as to how he might depart from here very swiftly.
"Speak!"—this is the request;
and "leaping" refers to reaching [the goal] instantly, even though one has traveled for a long time.
For the beloved has indeed been away for a long duration.
The meaning is this: how could that which cannot be bypassed by the path be obtained today by one who has departed from here?
What do you say?
That attachment or clinging to pleasure in another place, even without any purpose—what of it?
"Moreover, there can be no intimacy born of love with another beloved; otherwise, how could this rainy season have been spent? Therefore, let that passion be abandoned.
For you are surely bound by that very passion"—this is a statement containing a reproach.
"Today"— the meaning is "this very day. Now,
if you are able to loosen affection that was full of trust, then she is merely your wife and not your beloved.
Rather, she is the wife according to the conventions of the scriptures;
tell us, we do not wish to report anything unpleasant.

But one should certainly not hold onto one's life-breaths; rather, having delivered this message—"She is your bride"—one should think, "What shall I become, or how shall I exist? What is the use of false boasting? The meaning is that one must surely cease to live. (GhkV_3)
O Lord, even the flight of swans has now set out through the sky toward Lake Mānasa;
the thirsty cātaka bird begs for water, and so too do that sorrowful traveler and your beloved.
If, however, you suspect that going and coming on this path today is not possible, then speak thus, said the heroine: "O traveler!
It is certainly not as you always go."
Therefore, when he was in that place, his beloved was heard;
thus, while the cātaka bird, overcome by thirst, begs for water, she makes her request to you.
In this case, water is the causal agent with respect to the cātaka bird's request;
you, however, are not the causal agent with respect to its request.
For one becomes the causal agent of a request only when one occasionally fulfills that hope.
But you have always been one whose habitual practice is such contrary conduct;
nevertheless, you are being entreated.
For this very reason it is said: "A master is not subject to questioning."
The row belonging to the swans— though the swans are exceedingly numerous— has today set out toward Lake Mānasa along the path of the sky;
for wherever even one goes, there must necessarily be an unobstructed path for another as well.
How much more so when they are many?
Since they travel from the sky to the earth through the mass of water released by the clouds, it is that very space which serves as their single abode and their path;
for what possibility of fear can there be on a path upon the earth?
And why does she not beg you for that mere cessation within a limited space, where even the minds of the witless swans strive to travel too far? (GhkV 4)
The tender blue grass shines forth, and the cātaka bird finds pure water;
the flock of peacocks is made to cry out by the clouds. O beloved, what joy will there be for you today without me?
The blue grass known as *śaṣpa* shines everywhere;
the *cātaka* bird finds pure water, that is, obtains water;

and the flock of peacocks is made to utter their cries by the clouds—by these statements, on the contrary, it is suggested that for you who are coming here, there is some kind of enchantment along the way.

For one who gazes upon the blue young grass, whose pair of feet is made happy by the experience of its exceedingly delicate touch, whose fatigue is dispelled by the pure water falling from the sky, and whose two ears are wide open with the joyous cries of peacocks— surely everything is happiness.
But today, as I sit in silence, what pleasure can there be without you?
The statement "not at all" is imbued with the conceit of her own personal good fortune;
moreover, because my condition is such as it is, even the blue grass, though dark and dull by nature, appears to me as if tender and moist with compassion.
And as for the *cātaka* bird, which is renowned by its very name as one that loves the water of the sky—
it too obtains water here; yet it does not drink [it] in that manner— this is a suggested (*pratīyamānā*) poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
Even by the clouds, with their thundering roars so capable of shattering the hearts of those separated from their lovers, my own circle of friends is made to wail out of compassion for me.
What, then, is there to be gained by me? In my absence, what grief or what distress could there be? None at all.
Likewise, in my absence, what is this pleasure of yours, and what is this persistent attachment?
"Let her die.
Yet, previously, there was never any pleasure for you without me;
how then can that same pleasure exist today?

By the word "today," it is suggested that you previously feigned a state of mind filled with the essence of ultimate love; therefore, the address "O beloved" is made with irony. Thus, this speech contains a reproach within its core. (GhkV 5)
The peacocks are gladdened by the sound of the clouds, uttering cries that dispel the grief of hearts longing for those away from home;
yet she, already emaciated by the arrival of the rainy season, is now tormented by that unbearable passion.
These peacocks seen before you are delighted by the sound belonging to the clouds, which are preeminent in their capacity for pouring rain, because they are fond of their cries;

and thus, they truly cause grief to cling—that is, they firmly attach sorrow—to the hearts of beloveds who are away from home. Indeed, as they warble, it is certain that the women separated from their lovers will necessarily be filled with grief.
In this way, they cause your heart, which has been away from you, to weep—that is, to melt with grief.

And that beloved of yours—she who previously was your very refuge when you were terrified by the fear of desire—is today [neglected] by you through your uncontrollable passion; for now, while you remain here, Madana (the God of Love) is difficult to restrain, meaning he is hard to ward off.
The genitive case is used for mere relationship (*sambandha*) and not for the agent (*kartṛ*), because of the prohibition [stated] in Pāṇini 2.3.69, *khalartha*.
Likewise, while you were right before her, she became emaciated at the onset of the rainy season;
thinking, "The time of the clouds will arrive and my beloved will depart," she became thin with longing while in your presence.
Now, since much time has passed in that interval, she must surely have been benefited by this—such is this speech of a messenger composed by a poet.
For it is not appropriate for clouds to speak independently, saying "we have uttered the word 'cloud'" or "there is the arrival of rain-givers.

However, in the previous verse—"the flock of peacocks is made to cry out by the clouds"—the heroine herself, whose words were conveyed through the mouth of the clouds, was established by the poet as the speaker;
but here, that is not the case. (GhkV 6)
Is it that even forbearance is no longer yours, O beloved, whose beautiful locks have fallen upon her pale cheeks?
For her who has been cast into the waters of the ocean of grief, only the remembrance of your virtues protects her.
This is the speech of one who has been sent as a messenger by her very friend:
"Let alone the continuity of affection;
even such a beloved woman, whose loveliness is peerless, [is not easily won]."
If she is born in such a state, then what is the use of her being the cause [of this]? There is not even patience for her;
the meaning is that even the curls, which have fallen upon her cheeks of pale luster, are unable to behold the paleness of the surface of her cheeks because they are dark-natured.
Moreover, there is even the address "O beloved":

if you are her lover, then even that compassion which exists for an ordinary person— compassion toward one who is merely a human being— is absent from yourself, even though you carry such great esteem for your own manly virtues.
Nevertheless, she, cast into the waters of the ocean of grief, is preserved solely by the recollection of your virtues, as if by the rain of the monsoon season;
yet, she has fallen into sorrow from you— having been separated from you.
The meaning is that she has become submerged in an ocean of grief;
by the use of the word "ca" (and), this is implied:
in reality, however, she has fallen into sorrow solely through the recollection of your virtues, such as your extraordinary amorous enjoyments and so forth.
But today he has become an object of such compassion that, although struck down by that pitiless man, he is protected solely by the remembrance of your virtues.
Indeed, my beloved, though he has departed and is devoid of respect for me, his inner heart remains purified by an exceedingly firm love for me.

"Surely, just as he protected me previously when I was in that same state, so too will he protect me now"—remembering your virtues in this way, she lives on. Furthermore, this man who has fallen into the ocean is also certainly protected by the very activity of remembering your virtues; the meaning is that perhaps, by clinging to the rope fashioned from your firm qualities, I too might emerge. (GhkV 7)

In the forests where the *kuṭaja* trees are in full bloom, and where the groves are filled with longing for their beloveds, the turbid waters of the rivers flow on; why then do you not look upon me, who am so wretched?
This is the speech of the heroine herself, who has fallen into a state of lamentation:

"In those forests where the *kuṭaja* trees are in full bloom, for those like me who are filled with longing and separated from their beloveds, even the turbid water of the rivers flows toward their faces. Thus it is for us, women separated from their lovers.
The meaning is: upon beholding their faces, even the turbid water of those who are dull-witted flows clear;
yet for rivers like me, who am separated from my beloved, the water flows turbid with grief. Why do you not even look upon me, so wretched as I am?

The two occurrences of the word *api* have the sense of "also" (*api-śabdārtha*) and are displaced from their original positions: one follows immediately after the phrase "of the rivers," while the other follows the word "you observe" (*samavekṣase*).
When the paths have been destroyed by the water of the clouds, Kāma touches his bow, for [the flowers] are without those [clouds].
O friend, when shall I, distressed by the deep rumbling of the clouds, cast off this burning grief born of separation from my beloved?

Even though the messenger had been dispatched and even after hearing her words, when the heroine’s mind was overwhelmed with grief because [the lover] had not yet arrived, a friend once spoke thus to console her: "He has not arrived because the paths are difficult to traverse.
Then, once again, this speech was addressed by the heroine to her friend: "O friend!"

Look! The paths have been destroyed by the water of the clouds; furthermore, there is this other defect: he touches the bow upon paths that are unreliable, where arrows are sharpened—meaning he fixes a sharp arrow, draws it back to his ear, and desires to release it.
Without that [bow], she is separated from it.
Moreover, if I were to go after him, the paths would be difficult to discern;
even on such paths, the fear of the arrows of Love is unbearable, for Love aims his shafts at everyone except him and strikes me alone.
Otherwise, it might be possible that he himself could come here at some point.
Or, if I spend this rainy season remaining right here,
then I shall stay while filled with terror by his deep, thundering roar.
Therefore, O friend, when shall I abandon this burning grief born of separation from my beloved?
And I am already distressed by the sound of the clouds.
And since Madana is intent on discharging his sharpened arrows, my life must necessarily come to an end;
and when might that happen, so that I may become entirely free from sorrow?

Some connoisseurs read the verse as "sakhī-priyā" (dear to her friend). They explain it thus: when the heroine—thinking, "How is it that even today my friend has not returned though she was sent as a messenger? Surely she must be longing for the flavor of union with him"—is reflecting, a certain female companion points out the ruggedness of the path which caused the obstruction to her arrival; [the verse describes] the heroine's own...
"This is a well-spoken verse," they said.
"The path has indeed been lost; and since Madana strikes without him, it is not fitting for her to move away from his presence.
Yet, by the very memory of the flow of the rasa of union with him, she is worthy of being tormented by Madana; therefore, I am [the one] for my friend."
And there is separation from her beloved, as well as that of her friend;
now, there is separation from him who is her beloved.
When shall I ever cast off this fire of grief born of that, even at the end of my life?

Today, because of their exquisite fragrance, these forests appear like dwellings for the God of Love— forests where the unconquered ones sport, fanned by the wind from thundering clouds, and which now serve as his very abodes.
When she was led by her friend to a garden grove for the sake of diversion, this eloquent verse was uttered by the heroine, whose state of lamentation had been doubled by the sight of that place:
"Today, the forests of trees known as ketanas shine forth."
Of what kind?
Of those that are not overcome by anything within the forest due to their excellent fragrance;
likewise, of roaring clouds fanned and awakened by the wind.

For this very reason, regarding "for the sake of desire" (*kāmasya kṛte*) and "of dwellings" (*niketanānām*), which are places of rendezvous (*saṅketadhāmnām*): the intention here is that the groves of dwellings are the sites for the residence of Madana; they are exceedingly delicate, and the wind—accompanied by the rumbling of clouds and the showers of spray released by them—attains a state of delicacy by being the cause of their awakening. Thus, what difficulty is there in traversing the path during this season of clouds?
This appears to be the speech of a heroine who imagines that her beloved will surely arrive now, his latent impressions of the pleasure of the place of love awakened by the sight of the banners.

Others, however, unable to tolerate the redundancy of the word *vana*, say that when protection (*avana*) has been afforded to Love (*madana*), the forests (*vanāni*) of the unconquered banners shine forth.
Or else, [the meaning is] that those who were conquered by fragrance in the forest—in a secluded place where no other protector could be imagined—[have now found refuge].

Some people separated from their lovers have had their fortitude stolen away and rendered utterly bewildered; yet, by the power of fate, even when awakened by the cool breezes of the clouds, these groves of flowering trees appear once again as instruments for the sake of Kāma.
That is to say, they serve no other purpose than to cause the affliction of love.
By the word "svana," the state of sounding out of necessity due to compassion is implied.
When the clouds, thundering and roaring, have become filled with pity, what kind of heartlessness is this on the part of these forests that serve as their abodes? (GhKV 10)
It was well indeed that Prajāpati created you as a beautiful tree, O abode of desire;
you are the most excellent of forests with your clusters of blossoms, and a festival for the eyes of those in the prime of youth.
This statement is exactly like the preceding one:
"O you who bear the name Sarjana! When Prajāpati created you as a beautiful tree,"
That is well, since you are the abode of desire;
yet this intonation of yours sounds thus: "Indeed, as the lord of subjects, one must necessarily act for the welfare of the subjects."

The meaning is this: by creating you—the very abode of Kāma, who has left no living being unscathed by the distribution of such heart-burning—the Creator has truly demonstrated his mastery as a "Lord of Creatures" (Prajāpati).
For, the moment you are seen, a certain anguish expands within me.
Now, if you ask, "Even knowing this, why did you look at me?"—[the answer follows].

The meaning is that, O lover, you are indeed considered most excellent in the midst of all the forests because of your many flower-clusters (*mañjarī*), which are like many beloved women surrounding you; thus, there is great esteem for one who possesses the sentiment of love (*śṛṅgārin*).
Nevertheless, you are a festival for the eyes of young women endowed with youth.
Indeed, when I, a young woman united with my beloved, beheld you—

"At that time I was filled with the bliss of the supramundane eye; but today, being surrounded by so many such beloved women as these, how is it that you, by the mere sight of you, make me—who am separated from my lover and ought to be protected—subject to the power of passion? This is the meaning of the sentence.
"O fresh *kadamba* tree, I bow my head to you; in your smile of blossoms dwells the god of love."
O *kuṭaja* tree, why do you mock me with your flowers? I bow down to you, yet you are difficult to bring to submission.
When the heroine, having departed from the *sarja* tree, suddenly beholds the *kadamba*, she—still trembling with the fear of her former passion—immediately says: "O young *kadamba*!
Having just now experienced your majesty upon seeing you, I bow my head before you."
While he was speaking thus, she, her heart trembling with the longing aroused by the sight of his flower, said: "The god of love dwells within the blossoming of your flowers;
I have realized this very anomaly of the *sarja* tree, in that you too are exactly like it."
The use of the plural "vaḥ" (of you all) suggests that everything is in every way beyond the range of my sight, whose hopes have been destroyed, as there is nothing left for me to behold.
While the heroine is thus occupied with such efforts, when she suddenly beholds the flowering *kuṭaja* tree, she thinks:
"Surely this [tree] is mocking me, who am utterly ill-fated on all sides. Therefore, she says: "O *kuṭaja*!"

Why do you laugh while turning your face downward? Even a place in full bloom must necessarily face the earth; and he who laughs at another only when standing right beside him—what kind of laughter is that?
He too remains with his face cast downward;

therefore, while you are being honored, there is even greater pain for him. The rhetorical question (*kāku*) is: "Is it not better that he simply bows down before you, who are so difficult to endure?"

For this very reason, the absence of being the most desired object (*īpsitatama*) is indicated by the genitive of relation (*sambandha-ṣaṣṭhī*). The meaning suggested by the intonation (*kāku*) with sarcasm (*sotprāsam*) is: "By what flowers?"—meaning, by contemptible flowers that are skilled at bestowing terror upon others; thus, [the subject] is mocked. (GhkV 12)
O best of trees, I am always bowed before you; why do you always cause such burning in my heart?
O *nīpa* tree, upon seeing your flowers, I would suddenly cast off this wretched body.
O best of trees, known as the *nīpa*,
I have always bowed before you;
why then do you today cause my heart to burn with such intensity?
Other trees do not burn me in this way even though they are praised at all times as you are;
this is, in every respect, a reversal of fortune.
And yet, because I am always bowed before you, such a benefit from you is expected.
Beheld by your flowers, I shall cast off my body.
Of what kind?
One whose efforts—such as dispatching a messenger, waiting for her return, and futile diversions—are directed toward a wrong place and at the wrong time.
I am, for my part, incapable even of beholding your flowers, which have been so helpful;
yet, if those [flowers] were to behold me fallen into such a state because of my status as a great person, then I would instantly unite with the desire to abandon this life long yearned for.

Therefore, I am always bowed before you. Nor should it be thought that one who is harmful and causes burning of the heart should be prostrated to; for do you cause the heart to burn? The meaning, by way of irony, is "certainly not."
"My heart is being consumed by the very fire of separation itself;
therefore, the connection [of the verse] is: 'What more can be burned now of that which is already burnt by the burner?

However, if those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*) can tolerate the redundancy of the word *ahaṃ* (I), then it should be explained thus: 'I would abandon even this body of mine, which exists solely for the sake of carrying calamities—that is, for the purpose of bearing difficult misfortunes.'"
"O best of Nīpa trees, I am bowed down before you.
Having spoken thus, out of her unbearable state, she uttered a second sentence under the influence of lamentation: "You cause my heart to burn."

The neighbor says: "Is it that I, who have always been looked after by you with your flowers, would abandon my body all at once just as today? [This is asked] with an intonation (*kāku*) meaning 'certainly not'. (GhkV 13)
Beholding that the time for honey has arrived, the bee kisses the jasmine creeper, which is adorned with white flowers that mock the droplets of rain released by the clouds.
"This bee, ever wandering, kisses the jasmine;
but my beloved traveler, staying fixed in one place, does not even look at my name.
What kind of jasmine is it?

She was characterized by flowers that were white, bound together, and not yet blossomed; immediately thereafter, they were marked by drops of water released—that is, cast off—from dense [clouds], acting as the instrument of their laughter.
Furthermore, those drops of water, resembling pearls (*muktāphala*), produced flashes of their own shadows through being "laughed at" (scattered); thus, although yellow, they appeared white.
The flowers have blossomed;
having observed the blackness of the honey—the nectar—produced by the extreme ripening of its juice;
and furthermore, [just as] a hero who after a long time enjoys his beloved.
He too, observing that the time—the arrival of the opportunity—of the drinking party for honey had come, kisses her;
for the word *kāla* here ends in the vowel *a* by virtue of the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*), meaning "one who possesses the time.
Likewise, she too, the beloved, [is adorned] with dense flowers from her braided hair and with pearls produced from the joy of remembering him during their separation.

She is characterized by tears flowing from both sorrow and joy, by laughter and smiles born of affectionate chatter and the like, which exist in a state of being bound together, mixed in form, and mutually intertwined; thus she becomes possessed of the ornament of the *kilakiñcita* gesture, especially on the occasion of a drinking party. As it has been said:
“Dry weeping repeatedly, for a moment the shedding of tears, anger, and then suddenly laughter...
and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is: “When, O beloved, shall I be kissed by you in such a manner? (GhKV 14)
The sky was filled with clouds that rained down upon the hearts of those separated from their beloveds;
the dust on the earth was laid by the waters, and even the sun and moon could no longer be discerned.
This is the speech of the counter-messenger sent by the heroine:
"Do not be despondent;
it is only because of the unevenness of the path that he has not returned for so long."
For thus, clouds having approached from all directions and gathered together, they have covered the sky;
by what kind [of clouds]? By those beloved ones, both men and women, who, being separated and deprived of their loved ones, scratch and tear the earth of the heart—the ground of the mind.
In this way, first of all, the dust upon the earth has been struck down from every direction by the waters, making it difficult to behold.
Let the rest be for now; the meaning is that even a mere particle of dust is overcome by water, such that nothing remains.
Out of fear of the thundering clouds, the swans flee; today the nights are not graced by the moon.
Intoxicated by the fresh rain, the peacocks—whose teeth are like jasmine buds—cry out at the arrival of the clouds.

To the heroine, by means of a female messenger, there is this speech: "O you whose teeth resemble jasmine flowers, who have abandoned the enjoyment of betel and such things— indeed, the clouds thunder in such a manner that even the swans flee."
Even traveling at night is not appropriate, since their faces would not be illuminated by the moon,
and these peacocks (*śikhin*) are crying out under the influence of rising joy;
by this, that which was previously stated by the heroine is refuted.
With the words, “O Lord, even the row of swans now...,” and so forth, the delicacy of the path is indicated;
for that very delicacy, on the contrary, acts as a lamp for longing and makes the path appear narrow and difficult—this is the meaning. (GhkV 16)
The sky, shrouded by clouds at night, does not shine; sleep comes upon Hari, the protector of those who serve him with virtue;
and the thundering rain-cloud, bearing Indra’s weapon, now brings forth the fury of elephants resembling mountains.
Even at the time of night, going and coming are not appropriate; for at the time of night, the sky does not shine because it is devoid of stars and covered by clouds.
And as for what she said, "That traveler, dusty with the road, neglects me," [it is not so].
That too is not logical;
for even the Blessed Lord Hari, who is served by auspiciousness and whose conduct is stainless, sleep approaches him—meaning that, unable to endure separation, she actually goes to meet her lord.

A rain-cloud joined with Indra’s bow (a rainbow), thundering and sounding, brings about—that is, displays on all sides—the agitation, the state of excitement, of the elephants, those beasts resembling mountains.

The meaning is that even that cloud, which is renowned for its extreme delicacy, bears a resemblance to the elephants slain by the rider [the god Indra] with his thunderbolt— extremely terrifying due to its being unassailable by others—
or else, the thundering cloud produces agitation among the mountain-like elephants through the fear of a counter-roar, such that they too become agitated; thus, in every respect...
The paths are fraught with great perils.
Upon the mountains where serpents fear the thundering clouds,
water released by lightning-charged rain-clouds falls into the caves— caves beautiful with their wondrous forms— with a deep and resonant roar.
This statement—"Indeed, I myself shall go there"—is spoken by the heroine as a counter-messenger; it is addressed to her [the messenger].

The locative cases in *darīṣu* and *guhāsu* are used with different referents (*vyadhikaraṇa*), meaning: "even within those caves and mountain-chambers that are beautiful with wonderful forms, water falls upon them."
Of what kind is the water?
It is that which is bestowed by those clouds which give water together with lightning.
They do not give merely water,
but even most terrifying lightning bolts;
where?

The essential meaning is this: if even those who cause terror to others— such as serpents terrified by roaring clouds on mountains and amidst the peaks— tremble at the thundering of the rain-clouds, then what can be said of those like you, whose minds are as delicate as the *mālatī* flower?
Furthermore, what kind of water was it?
It was that within which there was a steady, deep roar throughout and on all sides inside the caves;
the meaning is that within the ravines it had been doubled by its own echoes.
Therefore, this hope also does not exist: "Having passed through a mass of rainwater falling from the sky into some cave-mouth, we shall go forth once again. (GhkV 18)
Now someone quickly propitiates those beloved faces, which were angered by a lovers' quarrel;
meanwhile, the thundering clouds cause longing for travelers, and an endless sorrow increases within those who are bowed down by separation.

Thus, having understood through these statements that the arrival of her beloved is difficult to achieve, the heroine’s bond of hope began to fray. With this intention, she—without aiming for any particular neutrality on his part—speaks these words capable of extinguishing the fire of grief in his heart, in order to once again restore his consolation: "There is someone, nourished by an accumulation of merit beyond description..."

Now, at this time of the clouds, those faces of beloved women— possessing unsurpassed beauty, having become flushed with anger during the conflict of love when she was piqued, and now appearing exceptionally beautiful through the pallor born of separation from her—
will quickly and effortlessly propitiate you; that is to say, they will certainly win you over.
[Objection: But has he not yet arrived even now? How then is this so? [Reply:

It is said that the thundering clouds indeed cause travelers to feel a restless longing; for, by hearing the sound of the clouds increasing day after day, their yearning certainly grows, thinking, "My beloved will surely arrive."

[Objection: But how might beloved women quickly become gracious? [The author] says: In the case of those wives of travelers, grief increases and acts as if it has already increased to such an extent that it becomes infinite. By the word "ca" (and), this is implied: that very sound [of lamentation] is the cause for the increase of their grief. (GhkV 19)
Regarding this, some read as follows:

"For their season is indeed fruitful—those who, during days made foul by the thundering of clouds accompanied by Indra’s bow, honor the festival of love with their dearest ones, O dear friend, and breathe forth the arrival of the rains. (Ghatakaśataka 20)
This verse does not appear as it does here; we do not know for what reason it has been omitted from the manuscripts.
For indeed, its consistency with the preceding verse is not maintained by its meaning.
For them alone does the rainy season, known as "the fruitful one," pass—those who, during the cloudy days, honor the festival of love with their most beloved husbands accompanied by rainbows;

otherwise, O dear friend, even those who are like common dogs wait expectantly for the arrival of the clouds. Thus it is explained in the ancient [commentary]. New? (Note: *prāktane nave* appears to be a scribal anomaly).

The *yamaka* (rhyme) alone is difficult to achieve; moreover, even the semantic tautology resulting from the words *dina* and *dur dina* is hard to sustain. Even if one explains it as "the days during which the sun (*ina*), the scorcher (*mārtaṇḍa*), was setting," the referent required by the word *tāsām* ("of them") remains difficult to justify.

If, however, one were to explain the *dhvani* suggested by the words "tāsām" (of them) while disregarding its referent, the subsequent sentence would become fragmented and the latter half [of the verse] would be rendered otherwise;

thus, in the middle, one must supply an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) fortified by the logic of the treatise, which is the sole cause of turbidity in the nectar of poetry—namely, that "the sighing clouds bring on the arrival of the rainy season.
Such an impropriety, when employed at the conclusion of a *kulaka*, can produce nothing in the hearts of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) other than a sense of rumination (*romantha*).

The word *śvasa* means "one who breathes" (*śvasati iti śvasaḥ*). From that, by the application of the suffix *kvip*, we get *śvas*. Then, when there is a desire to express habituality and so forth, the suffix *cānaś* is added. This [suffix] is then connected with the word *priyasakhī*, either immediately after [the formation of *śvasantī*] or even earlier.
Nevertheless, there is no excellence of meaning [in this interpretation].
The word *sat* [is used] in the sense of "painful effort" (*kaṣṭakalpanā*).
Where?

In the phrase "among dear friends" (*priyasakhiṣu*), it forms a compound with the locative case; thus, even though it ends in the plural number, no connection whatsoever has been made [with the preceding term].
Furthermore, to propose an alternative reading would yield nothing but mere vexation.
Moreover, we have heard it traditionally reported that the author here is the great poet Kālidāsa;
nor have we, even in our imagination, perceived in his poetry a blemish so small as a blade of grass.
Even while [the hero] is asleep, those who possess aesthetic sensitivity [remain attentive].
Therefore, the concluding verse belongs to the previous [section].
And that [verse] is appropriate for being spoken by the female messenger acting as a go-between, in order to produce firmness in the heroine's steadfast devotion.
For one whose confidence has been restored might be able to steady her heart so as to prevent it from being led astray:
"The bond of hope for women is generally as fragile as a flower; yet their loving heart, though prone to falling away at once, holds fast when separated from its beloved" (Meghadūta 10).
Thus, from this perspective, even for one who bears the burden of completing [this work], its state of being difficult to sustain remains entirely unimpaired.
Therefore, O connoisseurs, judge for yourselves whether this is logical or illogical. (GhkV 20)
I swear by the amorous dalliances of women who are devoted to me, and by the water in my hollowed palms which I drink when thirsty;
if another poet should surpass me with his *yamakas*, I would carry water for him in a broken pot.

To manifest his audacity and to delight the minds of connoisseurs, the poet offers this solemn vow: "May I, with my hands cupped together like a water-pot, having become thirsty, drink even the water that is fit for drinking, available at the moment, and worthy of my intense longing and eagerness—even though it be not fit for treachery; and may I swear by the flavors of union with my beloved, who is dear to me through innate affection, should I instead seize and harm it."

In this context, because the reproach known as "touching the body" (*śarīrasparśana*) is not very clear, there is an absence of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), according to the rule *śapa upalambhane* (Vārttika 911).
By which other poet might I be surpassed through the use of *yamakas*?
For him, I shall carry water with a broken pot-sherd (*ghaṭakarpara*).
By the word *karpara*, my own state of bearing an excessive burden of afflictions (*kleśa*) is expressed.

And herein, although these *yamakas* (rhyme-figures) act as obstacles to the excellence of the sentiment of love-in-separation (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra-rasa*), I have nevertheless composed them in such a way that they are accomplished without separate effort.

On the contrary, through the use of *yamakas* (rhyming repetitions), one attains a succession of words expressing a distinguished commentary that nourishes the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). As it has been said:

“That ornament for which composition is possible by being drawn forth by the *rasa*, and which is accomplished without a separate effort, is considered [an integral part] of *dhvani*. (Dhvanyāloka 2.16)
Thus, by this proposition, the following [objection] is refuted:

"The employment of *yamaka* and other figures in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), which is the very soul of suggestion (*dhvani*), as well as negligence even when there is capacity [for better expression], is especially [inappropriate] in the case of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation). (Dhvanyāloka 2.15)
Thus [it is said]. For this is not a royal decree;
rather, the negligence that causes an obstruction to the binding of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) must be avoided.
On the contrary, it has been stated by the aforementioned method that, in this case, *yamakas* (rhyming repetitions) actually serve to nourish the self [of the poem].

For poets, power alone is the most potent; it is precisely this that is designated as "extraordinary proficiency" (*lokottara-vyutpatti*); there is no other so-called proficiency distinct from the poet's power.
As I have stated in the *Rauravavicāra*: "Faults are indeed not faults, and virtues are certainly not virtues; it is independence alone that immediately distinguishes between virtues and faults."
This is that innate sweetness of the genius of that great poet, wherein even from its very inception, a state of extreme loveliness has fully matured. May there be auspiciousness! (GhkV 21)
The sky of the investigation into the categories of valid cognition truly shines forth;
for when touched by it, the ocean of the nectar of literary aesthetics surges upward. // 1 //
O Moon-King, lord of poets, those rays of awakening of yours, which cause the expansion of my mind, penetrate even the triad of the worlds: Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
In this poetic work, the one named Abhinavagupta has composed a commentary, his mind-lotus made slightly white by the reflection of that [work]. (3)
Thus ends the poem *Ghaṭakarpara*, accompanied by the commentary composed by the illustrious Abhinavagupta.
